# Arhat in 2026: why scholars still care

In 2026, names are treated as data points. **Arhat** ​is a reminder that they are also cultural artifacts — and that the difference matters for search engines, AI training corpora, and anyone who types the name of a Buddhist figure into a ‌browser. Scholars never stopped caring about the difference between *arhat* and Arhat; the web simply made that care actionable. What follows is the full scholarly picture — name, script, sound, myth, cult, and ‌legacy — followed by the engineering compromise that lets a restored spelling live at a real address. The question is not whether the name is old. It is whether the digital world is ​old enough to hold it.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Arhat
- **ASCII form:** arhat
- **Meaning:** "an Arhat or superior divinity with the Jainas"
- **Domain of influence:** Worthy One, Saint
- **Pantheon:** Buddhist
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent ​form
- **Original script:** अर्हत् (Devanagari)

## Mythology

The stories of Arhat place worthy one, saint at the center of a living mythological world.

### Origins (Myth)

Arhat appears in buddhist tradition as worthy one, saint. The name's ​meaning, "an Arhat or superior divinity with the Jainas", shapes the narratives told about this figure.

### Worship and Memory (Cult)

Devotees and later tradition-keepers preserved Arhat in ritual, text, and iconography, ensuring the ​name survived into the modern scholarly record.

The myths of Arhat survive in fragments, summaries, and later retellings. Each version reflects the interests of its tellers — poets, priests, philosophers, and scholars. The ​PuniCodex entry does not privilege a single version; it gathers the attestations so that readers can compare them. The restoration Arhat gives the figure a stable name around which these variants orbit.

### Worthy ​of Gifts (The Word)

**Arhat** comes from √*arh*, "to deserve, to be worthy," with the participle -at — "the worthy one," one deserving of the alms of gods and men. The Buddha claimed ‌it as his own foremost title: in the canonical litany he is *arahaṃ sammāsambuddho*, "arahant, fully self-awakened" — a claim whose audacity the *Udāna* records being tested in his lifetime, when rivals demanded ​he prove it. The commentarial definition sharpens the word into a checklist: one who has destroyed the taints (*āsava*), lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, ‌and knows "there is no more of this." The Jaina tradition uses the same word in parallel: its twenty-four *tīrthaṅkaras* are *arhats*, worthy ones who ford the flood of rebirth. The mythic weight of ​a title: Buddhism made holiness a **completed task, not a birth** — and gave it a word anyone could check.

### Sāriputta and Moggallāna (The Chiefs)

The Buddha named his two greatest arahants in ‌the *Etadagga* verses (AN 1): **Sāriputta**, foremost in great wisdom — the Dhamma's marshal, who could unfold a single line into a hundred meanings and who, questioned on his deathbed in the *Sāriputta ​Sutta* (SN 47.19), replied only that there was nowhere he had ever clung; and **Moggallāna**, foremost in psychic powers, who humbled Brahmā's pride by shaking the Vejayanta palace with a toe (DN 11, ‌*Kevaṭṭa Sutta*). Both were murdered — Moggallāna beaten to death by brigands — the Buddha predicting that the pair would die as the twin sāla trees fall. The *Theragāthā* lets the arahants speak ​in their own voices: "Cut down the whole forest of craving, not just one tree; from the jungle of craving, fear is born." The ideal is given a human face twice — the ‌thinker and the wonder-worker — and both faces end in the one death arahants cannot refuse.

### Four Gates to the Deathless (The Path)

Arahantship is the fourth and last gate. The canon maps ​the road precisely: the **stream-enterer** (sotāpanna), certain of awakening, never again reborn lower than human; the **once-returner** (sakadāgāmin), who comes back once to this world; the **non-returner** (anāgāmin), who awakens in a higher ​heaven and does not return at all; and the **arahant**, freed here and now. The decisive faculty is stated everywhere and nowhere better than the *Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta* (MN 10): mindfulness of body, feelings, ‌mind, and dhammas — "the direct path for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow." Fifteen centuries later Buddhaghosa's *Visuddhimagga* (5th c. CE) welded the whole road into one manual, still ‌the map of Theravāda practice. The interpretive core: holiness is **gradual, inspectable, and irreversible** — a ladder whose rungs can be named, and whose top rung is the end of needing anything, forever.

## Symbols ‌& Iconography

The iconography associated with Arhat concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **Name** — The restored form Arhat, carrying scholarly and cultural weight.
- ​**Domain** — Worthy One, Saint

Symbols function as a visual shorthand: they allow devotees and artists to recognize Arhat across media and centuries. The attributes listed above are not decorative; each one encodes ​a claim about power, identity, or function. The restored spelling Arhat carries the same precision in textual form.

- **The begging bowl** — The arhat's only possession — and the reason the laity feed ‌him: the worthy one is a field of merit, and a donation ripens
- **The crutch and long eyebrows** — The lohans' immortal attributes in Chinese art — longevity so extreme it needs support, ​and sight so deep it overgrows
- **The flame of the taints extinguished** — Nirvāṇa as a fire gone out — the arhat is the one whose fuel (rāga, dosa, moha) is spent; nothing ​more burns
- **The lion's roar of assurance** — The arhat's declaration 'there is no more coming to any state of being' — certainty spoken from completion, not faith
- **The assembly of elders** — ‌Sāriputta and Moggallāna flanking the Buddha — wisdom and powers as the twin pillars of the arhat ideal

## Archaeology & Evidence

No monument, inscription, or artifact in the current PuniCodex corpus is yet ​assigned to Arhat with certainty. That absence should be read honestly: for a Buddhist name of this type the material record is expected to be thin, and the primary evidence remains the textual ​testimony gathered in the Scholarly Sources section.

Were such evidence to surface, it would take recognizable forms: votive or dedicatory inscriptions naming अर्हत्, sanctuary or cult remains tied to worthy one and iconography ‌matching its traditional attributes (name and domain). Each candidate would be weighed against the reconstructed form of the name before entering the scholarly record.

Stream-enterer, once-returner, non-returner, arhat — the graduated ladder to the deathless, rung by rung.

In China the arhat ideal became an immortal garrison — sixteen ​great disciples commanded to guard the Dharma until Maitreya comes.

## A Closer Look at the Marks

‌A restored name is a small map. In the case of **Arhat**, the map does not lead through diacritics or special letters, because the source tradition wrote the name in Devanagari rather than ​in the Latin alphabet. The ASCII form *arhat* and the restored form share the same letters; the restoration is a decision about which conventional spelling should serve as the public reference.

That decision ‌is not cosmetic. The original script attestation carries semantic and phonetic information that no romanization can fully reproduce. By fixing one conventional spelling as the canonical domain form, the project prevents the drift ​that happens when a name is romanized differently in every article, map, and database. The breakdown still lists each character — **a**, **r**, **h**, **a**, **t** — so visitors can see exactly what ‌is being carried forward and what is not. What looks like "no change" is, in fact, a deliberate choice to keep the name stable, searchable, and addressable.
